analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection queues are captured here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage projects waiting to connect to the grid as of September 1, 2026, spread across 8,379 individual requests. These are planned projects seeking a grid connection, not a count of data center demand, and the five queues cover different geographies under different rules, so their totals cannot simply be added to produce a single national figure. What they do reveal is the shape of investment pressure on the grid: solar dominates by capacity in ERCOT (151,883 MW), MISO (144,902 MW), and CAISO (18,896 MW), while NYISO's queue is overwhelmingly classified as "other" at 291,136 MW, and SPP carries the largest wind total among the five at 64,737 MW.

Storage and gas are the two fuel types most directly linked to the kind of firm, around-the-clock load that large AI data centers represent, because data centers cannot tolerate intermittency and grid operators increasingly pair reliable load growth with peaking gas and co-located battery storage. Across the queues that report them, battery storage requests total 160,906 MW in ERCOT alone, with another 68,429 MW in MISO, 52,913 MW in SPP, and 46,944 MW in CAISO — figures that reflect developers positioning to serve or support continuous industrial load. Gas interconnection requests, though smaller in absolute terms, remain substantial: 76,751 MW in ERCOT, 47,392 MW in SPP, 30,236 MW in MISO, 27,879 MW in NYISO, and 916 MW in CAISO, suggesting that in the largest load-growth regions developers are still filing for dispatchable thermal capacity alongside renewables.

The EIA commercial electricity sales data for June 2026 — a proxy for data center load rather than a direct measurement of it, since data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class — shows Texas leading reported states at 15,754 million watt-hours of commercial sales that month, followed by California at 10,025 million watt-hours and Virginia at 7,771 million watt-hours; average commercial prices ranged from $8.66 per kilowatt-hour in Texas to $27.33 in California, a spread that helps explain why so much interconnection activity is concentrated in lower-cost ERCOT territory. The alignment between high commercial sales volumes, low prices, and deep storage and gas queues in Texas, and between high prices and a storage-heavy queue in California, is consistent with data center developers and their utilities filing for the firm resources needed to serve growing loads, though the queue data alone cannot confirm that interpretation. Watch whether ERCOT's storage queue — already the largest single fuel-type total across all five operators — continues to grow in the October 2026 monthly report, which would be the clearest near-term signal that firm-load interconnection demand is accelerating.
